items.evidence: Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem.
items.note: The student clearly defines recursion as a self-calling function solving smaller instances.

items.evidence: Every recursive function needs a base case, which is the condition where it stops calling itself and returns a value directly.
items.note: The student explains the necessity of a base case to terminate execution.

items.evidence: The recursive step has to change the argument, like n minus 1, so each call gets closer to the base case.
items.note: The student explains that arguments must be modified to make progress toward the base case.

items.evidence: Each call is pushed as a new stack frame on the call stack, holding its own parameters and local variables.
items.note: The student covers how each call allocates a new stack frame for its parameters and variables.

items.evidence: When the base case is reached, the calls return one by one and the stack unwinds, and each caller uses the returned value to finish its own calculation.
items.note: The student describes stack unwinding and how values pass back through the call frames.

items.evidence: Recursion can be easier to read than a loop, but it uses more memory because of the stack frames.
items.note: The student compares recursion to loops, highlighting the memory overhead of stack frames.

target_reason: All rubric items have been fully covered by the student.
